name: Liam Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on response at Westbrook, the newest part of the city, all new estates, a retail park and a lot of young families. A typical shift is break-ins at the building sites, parking rows, car thefts from driveways, and a surprising number of online scams that end up with someone crying at their kitchen table. I like the variety and I like getting people their stuff back. What wears me out is how slow the force is with technology. The criminals are on encrypted apps and we're on a radio from 2009.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use technology yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: All the time. I use AI tools every day for my own stuff: budgeting, learning about investing, even planning the training sessions for the under-12s football team I coach. I bought a one-bed flat two years ago and rent it out, and I used an AI tool to check the lease. At work I'd use it far more if the force allowed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was useful but overhyped. At work I'd still push for better tools, because the scammers will use whatever's out there. Online I'd probably post something like, good tool, not a miracle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it suits me fine. The job's secure, I've got the rental flat and savings, and I'd keep growing that. I'd be a bit disappointed, because I'd hoped AI would drag the force into this century.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the fraud and cybercrime team, because scams are the biggest growth crime on my patch. I'd keep putting money into index funds and paying down the rental mortgage. And I'd keep coaching on Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit restless, maybe, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the scams on your patch.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month a retired couple on my patch lost 14,000 to someone pretending to be their bank. They'd saved it over thirty years. We got none of it back, and the gang was abroad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said restless. What would you want more of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Speed and ownership. I'd like to run something one day, a team or a business. I don't want to wait twenty years for a promotion because it's someone's turn.

say: AI was **useful but overhyped**, a good tool and not a miracle.
The force still needs **better tools**, because scammers use whatever's out there.
think: His **job is secure**, with a rental flat and savings behind him.
He's **disappointed** AI won't drag the force into this century.
do: Apply for the **fraud and cybercrime** team.
Keep paying into **index funds** and the rental mortgage.
S0.quote: Last month a retired couple on my patch lost 14,000 to someone pretending to be their bank.
fieldNote: He's motivated by **fraud victims** and getting their money back.
He wants **ownership** and speed, not a slow promotion queue.
His money is **already working**, through a rental flat and funds.

steps.text: Apply for the fraud and cybercrime team
Keep paying into index funds and the rental mortgage
Keep coaching the under-12s every Saturday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say about time. At work I'd tell people to get on board, because it's going to happen whether we like it or not. I'd also say the force should hire people who understand this stuff, not just buy it from a salesman.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me. The paperwork goes, which is a third of my day, and I'm already comfortable with the tools. The officers who refuse to learn will struggle, and honestly that's partly on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer for every AI pilot and push hard for the fraud team, where AI is used to trace money. I'd do an online certificate in digital investigation, about 800, out of my own pocket. And I'd look at starting a small business on the side with my brother Yusuf, who's an electrician, fitting smart security systems in homes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Energised. It feels like the kind of change that rewards people who move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the officers who refuse to learn are partly to blame. That's quite hard.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. I'm not saying leave them behind, the force should train everyone. But you've got to meet them halfway. My dad worked in a print works and retrained twice, and nobody handed it to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a side business allowed for a police officer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You have to ask permission and declare it, and it can't clash with the job. Fitting alarms and cameras is usually fine. I'd check with professional standards first.

say: It's **about time**, and colleagues should get **on board**.
The force should **hire people** who understand AI, not just buy it.
think: Losing the **paperwork**, a third of his day, is good for him.
Officers who **refuse to learn** are partly to blame, he thinks.
do: Volunteer for **every AI pilot** and push for the fraud team.
Pay about **800 for a certificate** in digital investigation.
Start a **smart security** fitting business with his brother.
feel: **Energised**, as if the change rewards **people who move**.
S1.quote: My dad worked in a print works and retrained twice, and nobody handed it to him.
fieldNote: He has a **self-reliant** view: meet the training halfway.
He sees AI as **a ladder** into fraud work.
He spots a **side business** with his brother Yusuf (an electrician).

steps.text: Pay for an online certificate in digital investigation

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, but I'd say it more kindly than that. At work I'd tell my shift to start learning now, today. Online I'd say the government should help people retrain, but people have to do their part too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one rattles me a bit. The thinking work, including the fraud work I want, goes to AGI in 2028. My hands-on side lasts until about 2031, when the robots come. So I'd have three years where the job is mostly being the human at the door, and then I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop counting on a police career and lean on the business side. Yusuf and I would get the security business running in the first six months, because people will want cameras and alarms when things feel unstable. I'd keep the rental flat, since people always need homes. And I'd use AGI tools for everything I can, from bookkeeping to marketing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not frightened. I've got options, and I'd rather be the one using the machine than the one replaced by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the security business. Wouldn't robots fit alarms by 2031 too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, yes. But by then I'd want to own the business, not be the one on the ladder. If robots do the fitting, I'd want to be the one who owns the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the people on your shift who can't do that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the hard bit. Some of them have kids and mortgages and no savings. I'd help where I could, but I can't carry everyone, and the government will have to step in somewhere.

say: It's **adapt** or get **left behind**, said kindly.
Government should help retrain, but people must do **their part**.
think: AGI takes the **fraud work** he wanted in 2028.
He'd have **three years** as the human at the door before robots come.
do: Launch the **security business** with Yusuf (his brother) within six months.
Keep the **rental flat**, since people always need homes.
Use **AGI tools** for bookkeeping and marketing.
feel: **Uneasy** but **not frightened**, because he has options.
S2.quote: If robots do the fitting, I'd want to be the one who owns the robots.
fieldNote: Fast AGI turns him from officer into **owner** almost at once.
His **assets** make him feel safe even when the job isn't.
He admits he **can't carry everyone** on his shift.

steps.text: Launch the home security business with Yusuf within six months
Keep the rental flat and its tenant

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty for anyone willing to work at it. At work I'd say let's be the force that gets this right first. I'd probably write something on the force forum about training plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is a good window for me. I'd be 32 when AGI hits and 35 when the robots come. I could have a few years on the fraud team, the business up and running, and maybe a second rental by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get onto the fraud team in year one and learn the AI tracing tools inside out. I'd start the security business with Yusuf part-time. I'd save for a deposit on a second flat. And I'd decide around year three whether to stay in the police or go full-time on the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Excited about the business, a little uneasy about the force.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a second flat rather than more savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Property is something you can see and touch, and even with AGI, people need somewhere to live. Funds go up and down, and I'd rather own a home than rent it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the under-12s you coach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn to work hard and learn to use the tools. Be the kid who asks how something works. That's the same advice whatever happens.

say: Five years is **plenty** for anyone willing to work at it.
Westbrook's force should be the one to **get this right first**.
think: At **32 and 35**, he'd have fraud experience and a running business.
He might have a **second rental** by then.
do: Join the **fraud team** in year one and learn the AI tracing tools.
Start the **security business** part-time with Yusuf.
S3.quote: Property is something you can see and touch, and even with AGI, people need somewhere to live.
fieldNote: He trusts **bricks and mortar** more than funds.
He sets a **year-three decision** on whether to stay in the police.

steps.text: Join the fraud team and learn the AI money-tracing tools
Run the security business part-time with Yusuf
Save a deposit for a second rental flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so nobody should be caught out. At work I'd say every officer should have a five-year plan. I'd keep my message simple: learn the tools, look after your money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm calm about this. I'd be 37 and 40 when it lands, probably with a family, a couple of properties and a business. The police might be part of my life by then, or might not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a full career in fraud for five or six years, maybe make sergeant. I'd build the business slowly and buy the second flat in about three years. I'd keep coaching. And I'd use every new AI tool the moment it comes out, like I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Positive, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could still go wrong for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interest rates are a bigger worry for me than robots. If rates jump, the flats get expensive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd do differently with ten years versus two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd jump straight to the business. With ten years I'd enjoy the police a bit longer, because I do love the job when it's going well.

say: Ten years is **a gift**, so nobody should be caught out.
Every officer needs a **five-year plan**, his simple message.
think: At **37 and 40** he expects a family, properties and a business.
The police may or may not **still be part** of his life.
do: Work in **fraud** for five or six years, aiming for sergeant.
Buy a **second flat** in about three years.
Build the **business slowly** alongside the job.
S4.quote: Interest rates are a bigger worry for me than robots.
fieldNote: His main risk here is **interest rates**, not AI.
Ten years lets him **enjoy policing** longer before switching.
He'd keep using **new AI tools** the day they arrive.

steps.text: Work in the fraud team for five or six years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, mostly for my colleagues. I'd be all right, I've got the flat and the business plan, but some of the lads on my shift have nothing behind them. What would help is the force paying for real retraining now, and making it easy for officers to start businesses or move into fraud and cyber work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the criminals. Whatever we get, they'll get first. That's the part nobody plans for.

headlineQuote: The criminals are on encrypted apps and we're on a radio from 2009.
portrait: Liam is a **27-year-old response officer** in fast-growing Westbrook who uses AI tools every day.
He owns a **rental flat**, invests, and coaches an under-12s football team on Saturdays.
He believes in **self-reliance**, and thinks officers must meet retraining halfway.
Fast AGI turns him toward a **security business** with his brother; slower timelines let him enjoy policing.
His biggest fear is for **colleagues** with nothing saved, not for himself.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, mostly for **colleagues** with no savings.
whatWouldHelp: Force-paid **retraining now**, with routes into fraud and cyber work.
Making it easy for officers to **start businesses**.
